This is a short tour that goes from raw data to a survival curve, a plot, and a fitted model. Each
step is only a few lines. The rest of the guide explains every piece in depth, and links are
collected at the end.

## Represent the data

Survival data pairs a follow-up time with an indicator of whether the event was actually observed or
the subject was censored (still event-free when we last saw them). Greenwood keeps the two together
in a `Surv` object. We use the bundled `lung` dataset, the survival times of patients with advanced
lung cancer. Since the data lives in a frame, we describe the response by its column names and let
Greenwood read them from the frame.

```{python}
# Import the Greenwood library
import greenwood as gw

# Load the bundled lung cancer dataset as a Polars DataFrame
lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars")

# Describe a right-censored response by column names, where a status of 2 marks a death
death = gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status")

# Evaluate it against the frame to see the Surv it produces
death.bind(lung)
```

The summary reports 228 patients, of whom 165 died during the study (the rest were censored).
`gw.Outcome.surv()` takes the same arguments as R's `survival::Surv()`, written as column names. One
detail to note: this dataset codes `status` as `1` for censored and `2` for dead (R's convention). As
in R, a `1`/`2` coding is recognized and passes straight through. The frame can be Polars, Pandas,
PyArrow, or DuckDB. When the values are already in hand as lists or arrays, `gw.Surv()` builds the
response from them directly.

## Estimate the survival curve

The Kaplan-Meier estimator turns those times into a survival curve, the probability of surviving
past each point in time. Printing the fitted estimator reports the median survival.

```{python}
# Fit the Kaplan-Meier estimator, reading the columns from the frame
km = gw.KaplanMeier().fit(death, data=lung)

# Print a summary: median survival with its confidence interval
km
```

The median is 310 days: half of the patients are still alive at 310 days. The two columns after it
give a 95% confidence interval for that median, 285 to 363 days.

## Plot the curve

The `plot_survival()` function draws the curve as an interactive chart, with a shaded confidence
band and a notch wherever a patient was censored.

```{python}
# Fit the Kaplan-Meier estimator
km = gw.KaplanMeier().fit(death, data=lung)

# Draw an interactive survival curve with confidence band and censoring marks
gw.plot_survival(km)
```

The curve starts at 1.0 and steps down at each death. It does not reach 0 because some patients were
still alive at the end of follow-up, so their survival time is only known to be at least that long.

## Model a covariate effect

To ask how a characteristic changes the risk of death, fit a Cox proportional hazards model. Here we
include `age` and `sex`, writing the model as an R-style formula. The response and the covariates
are read from the same frame, and any row with a missing value in a column the model uses is dropped
(the printout says how many). Printing the model shows a coefficient table.

```{python}
# Fit a Cox proportional hazards model with age and sex as covariates
cox = gw.CoxPH().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex", data=lung)

# Print the coefficient table and global test statistics
cox
```

The `exp(coef)` column holds hazard ratios. For `sex` (coded `1` for male, `2` for female) the
hazard ratio is about 0.60, which means women had roughly 40% lower risk of death than men over the
study, holding age fixed. A ratio below 1 is lower risk, above 1 is higher risk.

## Shared frailty for clustered survival data

If subjects are clustered (for example by center, family, or recurrent-event unit), you can make use
of the shared gamma frailty Cox model. As in R, a `frailty()` term in the formula names the cluster
column.

```{python}
# Shared frailty Cox model (clustered by institution)
cox_frailty = gw.CoxPH(ties="breslow").fit(
    "Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + frailty(inst)", data=lung
)

# Frailty variance inference (tests theta = 0)
cox_frailty.frailty_test()
```

See [Cox regression](08-cox-regression.qmd) for full guidance and interpretation.
